order.subject: science
order.topic: Chemical reactions and conservation of mass
order.requests: Follow my lesson notes. I never want a key or explanation that says mass disappears or that gas has no mass. Use the counting table I use for atoms.

itemRequests.notes: Fill-in blanks like my old notes, with a word bank and a Stop and think box per section.
itemRequests.slides: One slide per big idea, plus a closed vs. open flask slide. Speaker notes should tell me what to ask the class.
itemRequests.quiz: 10 questions, my Know it / Use it / Explain it parts. At least one balancing question and one open vs. closed mass problem. Include a picture with no answer labels.

notes: Name, Date and Period lines across the top, then the title and a "Science 8 · Mr. Okafor" line
Bold directions in one or two short sentences right under the title
Questions numbered 1), 2), 3) straight through the whole document, across parts
Multiple-choice letters in parentheses: (A) (B) (C) (D); circle the letter
Quizzes split into three parts: Part 1 · Know it, Part 2 · Use it, Part 3 · Explain it; Explain it asks for complete sentences and names the words to use in bold
Guided notes: ⭐ Key idea headings, short fill-in sentences with one blank each, a 🤔 Stop and think question, and a word bank used "only if you get stuck"
Plain, short grade 8 sentences; everyday contexts (a rubber duck, popcorn, a named student who makes a claim to check)
Teacher key: the letter, a short reason in parentheses for math steps, and "Look for:" points for written answers

documents.title: Chemical Reactions Review Game
documents.directions: Answer each card. Harder cards are worth more points.

questions.prompt: In the equation CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, which substances are the products?
questions.why: Products are the new substances, written on the right of the arrow: CO₂ and H₂O.

questions.prompt: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide. Which list names the reactants?
questions.why: Reactants are what you start with: magnesium and oxygen. Magnesium oxide is the product.

questions.prompt: What do we call the substances you start with in a chemical reaction?
questions.why: Reactants go in, on the left of the arrow; products come out, on the right.

questions.prompt: In CO₂, what does the small 2 tell you?
choices: There are 2 molecules of carbon dioxide in all.
The carbon atom is counted two times.
questions.why: The small number after a symbol is a subscript: 2 oxygen atoms in one molecule of CO₂.

questions.prompt: Use the counting table. How many atoms of each element are in 2Ca(OH)₂? Each answer lists Ca, O, H in that order.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 156" width="360" height="156" role="img" aria-label="Empty atom counting table: Ca, O, H" font-family="Arial, sans-serif"><text x="180" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2933">2Ca(OH)₂</text><rect x="0.5" y="34" width="359" height="30" fill="#e8eef5" stroke="#1f2933"/><text x="50" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">Element</text><text x="165" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">Reactant side</text><text x="295" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#1f2933">Product side</text><rect x="0.5" y="64" width="359" height="30" fill="#fff" stroke="#1f2933"/><text x="50" y="84" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2933">Ca</text><rect x="0.5" y="94" width="359" height="30" fill="#fff" stroke="#1f2933"/><text x="50" y="114" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2933">O</text><rect x="0.5" y="124" width="359" height="30" fill="#fff" stroke="#1f2933"/><text x="50" y="144" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2933">H</text><line x1="100" y1="34" x2="100" y2="154" stroke="#1f2933"/><line x1="230" y1="34" x2="230" y2="154" stroke="#1f2933"/></svg>
questions.why: The coefficient 2 multiplies everything: Ca 2 × 1 = 2; the parentheses hold O and H, each 2 × 2 = 4.

questions.prompt: How many hydrogen atoms are in 3H₂O?

questions.why: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO: Mg 2 and 2, O 2 and 2. Every row of the table matches.

questions.prompt: Which equation for rust is balanced?
questions.why: 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃: Fe 4 and 4, O 6 and 6. Every row of the table matches.

questions.prompt: Dev starts balancing Al + Cl₂ → AlCl₃ by writing a 2 in front of AlCl₃. He counts atoms and finds two rows that still don't match. Which change correctly finishes balancing it?
choices: Put a 2 before Al, then rewrite Cl₂ as Cl₆
Write a 2 before Al and a 3 before Cl₂
Write a 3 before Cl₂ but leave Al alone
Write 6 in front of Cl₂, then a 2 before Al
questions.why: After the 2 on AlCl₃: Al 1 on the left, 2 on the right; Cl 2 on the left, 6 on the right. Two coefficients are needed: 2Al + 3Cl₂ → 2AlCl₃ gives Al 2 and 2, Cl 3 × 2 = 6 and 2 × 3 = 6. A 2 before Al with Cl₂ rewritten as Cl₆ makes the counts match (Al 2 and 2, Cl 6 and 6) but changes a subscript, so it is no longer chlorine gas. A 3 before Cl₂ alone fixes Cl (6 and 6) but leaves Al unmatched (1 vs 2). A 6 before Cl₂ puts 12 Cl on the left against 6 on the right: the 6 is the count of Cl atoms needed, not the number of Cl₂ molecules.

questions.prompt: To balance an equation, you may change a subscript.
questions.why: Changing a subscript changes the substance. Balance by changing coefficients only.

questions.prompt: In a sealed flask, 12.0 g of substance A reacts with 5.0 g of substance B. Only one product forms. What is the mass of the product, in grams?
questions.why: Mass of reactants = mass of products: 12.0 g + 5.0 g = 17.0 g.

questions.prompt: In a sealed zip bag, 25.0 g of substance C reacts with 9.5 g of substance D. Only one product forms. What is the mass of the product, in grams?
questions.why: Mass of reactants = mass of products: 25.0 g + 9.5 g = 34.5 g.

questions.prompt: In a sealed zip bag, the mass after a reaction is the same as the mass before it.
questions.why: Nothing gets in or out of a closed system, so the same atoms (and the same mass) are on the balance.

questions.prompt: A class does the baking soda and vinegar lab in an open cup. The balance reads 120.0 g before and 118.6 g after. (a) What mass of gas left the cup? (b) Explain why the same reaction in a sealed zip bag would read 120.0 g after. Use the words mass and gas.
questions.answer: (a) 120.0 g − 118.6 g = 1.4 g of carbon dioxide gas. (b) In the open cup the gas escaped into the air, so the balance no longer measured its mass; the 1.4 g of gas is now in the air. In a sealed bag the gas is trapped, so all of the mass stays on the balance and it reads 120.0 g.
questions.why: Look for: 1.4 g; the gas left the open cup; the gas has mass and stays in the closed bag. A full answer never says the mass disappeared.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a chemical change?
questions.why: A glow stick gives off light because a new substance forms. Melting, dissolving and crushing make no new substance.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a physical change?
choices: A cake baking in the oven
questions.why: Cutting paper only changes its shape; it is still paper. Rusting, baking and burning make new substances.

notes: Capability fixture: a review game made from the g8-science sample quiz (both versions as their own cards, plus four short made-up cards; made-up teacher and students), in the interactive format, grading auto (the checks also build it graded "print"). Not a gallery sample.
